Mathematical finance

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Mathematical optimization
OurBigBook.com Words: 27k Articles: 477
Mathematical finance uses probability theory, linear algebra and mathematical optimization to study financial markets, portfolio decisions and contingent claim prices. One question asks which portfolio best serves a specified objective; another asks what price a contingent claim must have to exclude arbitrage. The latter can have an exact answer even when future stock prices are uncertain.
The central idea is claim replication: construct a self-financing portfolio delivering the same financial payoff as a contract in every possible state. The law of one price then identifies the contract's price with the portfolio's initial cost. The binomial market makes this beautiful connection between uncertainty and linear algebra visible using just two equations. Risk-neutral pricing expresses the same cost as a discounted expectation.
The one-step example below fixes today's stock price at 100, terminal prices at 120 or 80, and the bank account's gross growth factor at 1.05. A European call option with strike price 100 pays 20 or zero. Its replicating portfolio in a binomial market costs 250/21, independently of the physical up probability, provided both states remain possible. These are conclusions within the specified financial market model.

Dividend

Words: 48
Mathematical finance OurBigBook.com
A dividend is a payment to the holder of a financial asset in addition to changes in its quoted price. Under a continuous dividend yield δ, one stock unit produces cash δSt​dt, so its total gains are dSt​+δSt​dt. A self-financing portfolio must include this cash in its budget equation.

Financial volatility (σ)

Words: 48
Mathematical finance OurBigBook.com
Financial volatility quantifies variability of asset returns. In the Black-Scholes model, σ is the coefficient of the Brownian increment in the stock return dSt​/St​=μdt+σdWt​, so its instantaneous log-return variance rate is σ2. For deterministic time-varying volatility, the variance over an interval is the integral of that squared coefficient.

Drawdown (economics, Dt​=maxs≤t​ys​−yt​)

Words: 140 Articles: 1
Mathematical finance OurBigBook.com
The absolute decline from a previous running peak of a cumulative-value process. For positive peak values a relative decline can also be defined, but that is a different unit convention. Flat intervals do not end a drawdown, and a brief recovery that stays below the previous peak does not necessarily end it either. A maximum consecutive strictly negative run is therefore not generally a maximum drawdown.

Finite-horizon drawdown of a two-sign-memory process (Dmax​(N)=2⌊N/2⌋+2(N≥1))

Words: 74
Drawdown (economics) OurBigBook.com
For increments Xt​=at−2​at−1​+at​ with freely admissible starting sign history, the worst absolute financial drawdown over N steps is the displayed value. A four-state recursion dn+1​(b,c)=mina=±1​[dn​(a,b)+ab+c] computes the minimum cumulative increment, with zero initial costs. Mathematical finance OurBigBook.com
An arbitrage is an allowed self-financing portfolio with zero initial wealth, nonnegative terminal portfolio wealth almost surely under the physical probability measure P, and strictly positive terminal wealth with positive probability. In a finite model where every state has positive probability, nonnegativity means no loss in any state. Positive expected return alone does not establish arbitrage: losses may still occur.
For the binomial market example, suppose the European call option sells for 13 while its replicating portfolio costs 250/21. Sell the call, buy its replicating portfolio, and lend the surplus 13−250/21=23/21 in the bank account. The initial net cost is zero. At maturity the call obligation and portfolio cancel in either state, leaving (21/20)(23/21)=23/20. A price below 250/21 permits the reversed construction, using short selling and borrowing. This is the law of one price made operational; the assumed trading permissions are essential.

A risk-neutral measure Q is a probability measure equivalent to the physical probability measure P, meaning they agree on which events have zero probability. For assets without intermediate payments, prices expressed in the chosen numéraire must be martingales under Q. For a positive bank account B and a stock without dividends, this requires S/B to be a martingale; with dividends, use discounted dividend gains. In an unrestricted finite-state one-period financial market, existence of such a measure is equivalent to absence of arbitrage, by the fundamental theorem of asset pricing.
Physical probability p=P(up) describes the modeled frequency or belief about an up move. The risk-neutral probability q=Q(up) is constrained by traded prices. In the worked binomial market, q=5/8 even if p=1/2 or p=4/5. Calling Q risk-neutral does not assume that investors have no risk aversion; it changes the weights used for risk-neutral pricing.

If it is bounded below by a deterministic constant, that wealth is a supermartingale: add the lower-bound constant to obtain a nonnegative local martingale, then apply conditional Fatou to a localizing sequence. A zero-cost admissible portfolio therefore has expected discounted terminal wealth at most zero. Nonnegative terminal wealth with positive probability of a strict gain would have strictly positive expectation under the equivalent measure, a contradiction. Thus there is no admissible arbitrage. True martingales are not needed for this implication.

At each node a positive stock price moves to uSt​ or dSt​, with 0<d<u, while a bank account grows by a fixed gross factor R>0. Assume both successors have positive physical probability, no dividends, a frictionless market with no trading costs, divisible holdings, unrestricted short selling, and borrowing and lending at the same fixed R. A self-financing portfolio receives no outside cash after its initial funding; subsequent rebalancing uses its own proceeds.
This binomial market excludes arbitrage exactly when d<R<u. If R≤d, borrowing S0​ to buy one share gives terminal gains S0​(u−R) or S0​(d−R); these are nonnegative and one is positive. If R≥u, short selling one share and lending its proceeds gives the analogous arbitrage. Strict inequalities allow a positive risk-neutral probability for each state. The two traded payoffs also span both successor states, giving market completeness relative to the information generated by this tree.

A delta hedge long a derivative and short VS​ commodity units has riskless drift Vt​+21​σ2S2VSS​+δVS​ and value V−SVS​. Equating the drift to the bank return gives the displayed Black-Scholes equation. This is an additive cash carry term, unlike a proportional dividend or storage yield.
The corresponding pricing diffusion is dS=(rS+δ)dt+σSdW. A fixed-strike forward has value S+δ(1−e−rτ)/r−Ke−rτ, and put-call parity gives that same value for a matching call minus put. Greeks (finance)

The Greeks are sensitivities of a financial claim value to model inputs, expressed through partial derivatives. The option delta measures sensitivity to the underlying price; a delta hedge uses that sensitivity to cancel first-order price exposure.

Option theta (Θ=∂t​V)

Words: 91
Greeks (finance) OurBigBook.com
The derivative of an option's value with respect to calendar time at fixed current underlying price and other parameters. In the dividend-free Black-Scholes model, the Black-Scholes equation gives
Θ=ρ(V−xVx​)−21​σ2x2Vxx​.
(47)
The first term is the interest earned on the bond value of the replicating portfolio, while the second uses option gamma. A convex payoff with a short bond position has Θ≤0 when ρ≥0; a concave payoff with a long bond position has Θ≥0. Negative interest rates need not obey these signs: the affine payoff x−K has Θ=−ρKe−ρ(T−t). For a fixed payoff function, remaining-maturity sensitivity is −Θ.

Completing the square in the Gaussian exponent computes each truncated lognormal moment and yields the displayed formula, where d1​=(log(S/K)+(r+σ2/2)τ)/(στ​). Its terminal limit is 2(S−K)+​.

Binomial shout option with signed lock-in

Words: 98
American option OurBigBook.com
A holder may choose a shout time τ and receive max(ST​−Sτ​,0)+Sτ​−K=max(ST​,Sτ​)−K, or choose no shout and receive (ST​−K)+. The lock-in term is signed, so shouting below strike can create a negative payoff. Backward induction must compare this actual contract with waiting. For S0​=100, multipliers 1.1,0.9, bank growth 1.05, strike 101 and two periods, the optimal policy waits at zero, shouts after the first up move, and never shouts after the first down move. The risk-neutral price is 575/49. Claim payoffs at a recombined stock node can differ according to earlier shout history.

American call option OurBigBook.com
An American call option with no expiry. For geometric Brownian motion with drift r−y under a risk-neutral measure, positive dividend yield y, r>0, and volatility σ>0, let p>1 solve σ2p(p−1)/2+(r−y)p−r=0. Its value is (S∗​−K)(S/S∗​)p below S∗​=pK/(p−1) and S−K above. The power solves the stationary Black-Scholes equation with continuous stock dividends; value matching and smooth fit determine the threshold.
The candidate dominates the positive part (S−K)+ because its continuation branch is convex and tangent to S−K at S∗​. In the exercise region its discounted-generator residual is rK−yS≤0: the root equation gives yS∗​=K[r+σ2p/2]>rK. Applying Itô's formula to the discounted value, localized if necessary, gives an upper bound on every exercise policy. Stopping at the first hit of S∗​ attains it; on paths not yet hitting, the bounded discounted continuation value tends to zero. This supplies the optimal stopping verification. As y↓0, p↓1, the threshold diverges and the value tends to S.

Modern portfolio theory

Mathematical finance OurBigBook.com
Mean-variance optimization balances expected linear return against a positive-definite quadratic variance penalty.
Modern portfolio theory constructs portfolios by comparing expected return with variance risk and the effects of diversification.

Words: 55

The set of attainable return standard deviations and expected returns for budget-feasible risky investment portfolios. Negative weights are allowed when short selling is permitted. With positive definite covariance matrix and nonconstant means, the minimum-risk boundary is a hyperbola in standard-deviation/mean coordinates; its upper branch is the mean-variance efficient frontier. Adding a risk-free asset changes the budget constraint on risky holdings and produces a different attainable set.

Gaussian two-fund theorem

Modern portfolio theory OurBigBook.com
For nondegenerate Gaussian terminal prices, a finite maximizer of a differentiable increasing concave non-affine utility, subject to a linear budget, lies in the span of V−1s and V−1μ. Gaussian integration by parts gives
E[SU′(πTS)]=μEU′(πTS)+VπEU′′(πTS).
(52)
The budget first-order condition makes this a multiple of s. For a nonzero portfolio, non-affineness and the full Gaussian support imply EU′′<0, so rearrangement gives the span assertion. Affine utility is a genuine exception: when means are proportional to prices, every budget-feasible portfolio is optimal, including portfolios outside that span.

With fixed budget sTπ=x, positive definite covariance V, and mean vector μ independent of s, set A=sTV−1s, B=sTV−1μ, C=μTV−1μ and D=AC−B2>0. The minimum variance at mean m is the displayed parabola. Its upper-mean branch m≥Bx/A is efficient: the lower branch has a competitor with equal variance and higher mean. If μ is proportional to s, only one mean is feasible and this two-dimensional parabola degenerates.
The efficient frontier is the set of portfolios for which no other feasible portfolio has at least as much expected return and no greater variance, with at least one strict improvement.
